issues.legal_issue: A testamentary gift to a person described as an adopted son remains effective despite the adoption being invalid when the will and surrounding circumstances show that the person was designated to take personally rather than because of a valid legal status.
material_facts: The purported second adoption was invalid, and the will repeatedly described the intended beneficiary as the testator’s adopted son.
The will expressly excluded the first adopted son and his heirs from the testator’s property.
The testator had recently faced a challenge to the second adoption, but the compromise ending that litigation left the adoption’s validity unresolved.
The will made the beneficiary’s enjoyment depend in part on his conduct, indicating the testator’s concern with his character as well as his status.
The beneficiary remained in possession and enjoyment of the property for more than fourteen years after the testator and his wife died, without a claim by the excluded family members.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiary was intended to take as a designated person, notwithstanding the invalid adoption, and the will effectively conveyed the residue of the testator’s property to him.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a gift to someone described by a legal status depends on that status or is instead made to that person as a designated individual depends on the wording of the instrument and the surrounding circumstances. The distinction between language that merely describes the recipient and language that states the reason or motive for the gift is drawn from those considerations. The Court relied on Nidhoomoni Debya v. Saroda Pershad Mookerjee (1876) L.R. 3 I.A. 253 and Fanindra Deb Raikat v. Rajeswar Das (1884) L.R. 12 I.A. 72.

rule.if: succession_suit_challenges_will and invalid_adoption and will_excludes_other_claimants and adoption_challenge_left_unresolved and beneficiary_possessed_property_unchallenged

predicates.succession_suit_challenges_will: A succession proceeding challenges a will as ineffective because the beneficiary’s purported legal status is invalid.
predicates.invalid_adoption: The purported adoption through which the beneficiary was described in the will is found to be invalid.
predicates.will_excludes_other_claimants: The will expressly excludes other potential claimants from the property.
predicates.adoption_challenge_left_unresolved: A prior dispute raised the validity of the purported adoption but ended without determining that question.
predicates.beneficiary_possessed_property_unchallen: The beneficiary possessed and enjoyed the property for a substantial period without a competing claim from the excluded persons.

issues.definition: When a succession proceeding challenges a will because the beneficiary’s adoption is invalid, and the will excludes other claimants, the adoption challenge remained unresolved, and the beneficiary possessed the property without a competing claim, the will is effective for the personally designated beneficiary.

issues.legal_issue: A person is not liable as a trustee, or for a co-trustee’s breach, unless the evidence clearly establishes that the person became a trustee and accepted the obligations of that position.
material_facts: A compromise provided for money belonging to a minor to be invested in the minor’s name, to the order of two adults, who were to supervise or manage the investment; the wording was ambiguous about who had authority to operate on the money.
The hundi and compromise were read together, but the court found they did not clearly establish that one of the adults had the power to withdraw and control the deposited money.
The subsequent documents and conduct showed that the minor’s parents and the other adult arranged for collection and investment of the money through that adult’s firm.

The evidence did not show that the deceased adult directed or participated in those arrangements, accepted responsibility for the fund after collection, or knew of the other adult’s financial difficulties.
The claimant sought to recover from the deceased adult’s estate for the other adult’s alleged misuse of the minor’s money.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not prove that the deceased became a trustee or accepted responsibility for the fund, so the estate was not liable for the alleged co-trustee’s breach.
issues.legal_principle: Trusteeship is imputed only on clear and conclusive evidence of a transfer of ownership, the liability attached to that ownership because of confidence reposed, and the alleged trustee’s acceptance of that liability. Where the instrument is ambiguous, contemporaneous conduct may be considered in construing it, and the claimant bears the burden of clearly establishing trusteeship and liability. The Court considered sections 13(1), Explanation (iii), 8, 9 and 78 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and held that the rules concerning a person entitled under a negotiable instrument did not establish control over a later deposit receipt. It also referred to Krishnashet bin Ganshet Shetye v. Hari Valjibhatye (1895) I.L.R. 20 Bom. 488; Sethna v. Hemmingway, A.I.R. 1914 Bom. 286; In re Travancore National and Quilon Bank Ltd., A.I.R. 1940 Mad. 157; Arunachalam v. Vairavan, A.I.R. 1929 P.C. 254; Muthuraman v. Periannan, A.I.R. 1934 Mad. 621; and In re Beaumont, Beaumont v. Ewbank [1902] 1 Ch. 889. The Court further stated that a co-trustee’s liability for another trustee’s breach requires a contributing factor such as knowledge, connivance or gross negligence.

rule.if: trust_suit_seeks_estate_liability and ambiguous_investment_terms and subsequent_conduct_assigns_handling_to_another_person and no_clear_transfer_and_acceptance

predicates.trust_suit_seeks_estate_liability: A trust proceeding seeks to make an estate liable for an alleged trustee’s responsibility for another person’s breach.
predicates.ambiguous_investment_terms: The instrument concerning the fund does not clearly establish who had authority to control or operate on it.
predicates.subsequent_conduct_assigns_handling_to_a: The parties’ subsequent conduct shows that another person, acting with the beneficiaries’ guardians, collected and arranged the investment of the fund.
predicates.no_clear_transfer_and_acceptance: The evidence does not clearly establish that the alleged trustee received ownership or control of the fund and accepted the resulting fiduciary obligations.

issues.definition: When a trust proceeding seeks estate liability, the investment terms are ambiguous, subsequent conduct assigns the fund’s handling to another person, and no clear transfer and acceptance is proved, the estate is not liable for the alleged co-trustee’s breach.
